Morningstar sees 24% upside in Anthropic’s IPO range. The harder question sits inside the balance sheet: revenue is dominated by models less than six months old, while more than $900 billion of compute commitments remain binding for years.

That is not a normal growth mismatch. It is a duration mismatch between what must be continuously replaced and what cannot be easily canceled.

Revenue growth and model capability are fundamentals. So is the half-life of the product producing that revenue. Anthropic must repeatedly retire yesterday’s advantage, finance the next one, and honor infrastructure obligations made under an older technical map.

Demand can keep growing while flexibility disappears.

The serious valuation question is not whether Claude wins this cycle. It is whether Anthropic’s long-dated commitments leave enough room to survive every cycle after it.

research_bundle.summary: The strongest recent case is Anthropic’s 2026 IPO: explosive growth sits beside enormous infrastructure commitments and a product cycle in which models reportedly lose commercial relevance within six months. That makes organizational adaptation—not scale alone—the central competitive variable. Secondary cases reinforce the pattern: Klarna reversed a cost-first automation strategy after service quality deteriorated; Shopify’s CEO treated an AI-review question as norm-setting rather than measurement; and voter resistance to data centers shows environmental melt becoming a political constraint. Together, the cases distinguish rapid optimization from the capacity to convert disruption and error into durable structure.

Malik Ahmed Khan, CFA Nov 11, 2026 Share Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty On Tuesday, Anthropic provided an IPO range of $70-$78 per share, valuing the business at up to $1.4 trillion based on the fully diluted share count. The number is well below the $2 trillion valuation that the firm eyed back in September. Pricing is expected to occur on Nov. 18. Why it matters: We see Anthropic’s IPO range, and downward revision from September targets, as a reflection of the current market sentiment vis-à-vis artificial intelligence, not the firm’s fundamentals. The deal is being priced during a period of high market volatility, with investors increasingly souring on the AI trade. Amid concerns around data center construction and a potential slowdown in AI spending, investors are worried about the return AI labs will generate on their AI investments. This question matters to Anthropic, as the firm has more than $900 billion in compute commitments. The bottom line: Our fair value estimate for narrow-moat Anthropic is $92.0 per share, equal to $1.7 trillion in equity value. Using the midpoint of Anthropic’s range, we believe there is 24% upside to the firm’s shares, and we view the stock as undervalued. Our valuation of Anthropic stock is undergirded by robust top-line growth, with our forecast calling for a five-year revenue growth rate of 47% from 2027 to 2031. We see a healthy mix of deeper enterprise penetration, especially in the nearly 12,000 customers who are already spending more than $100,000 annually, as well as new logo wins to drive this top-line growth. Company Report: We See Anthropic as Well Placed to Capture Value in an AI World Anthropic: After the IPO, Who Controls the Company? Where Anthropic’s Revenue Goes, and Why It Matters Find Our Full Anthropic Coverage Here Bulls Say, Bears Say Bulls say: Our bull case for Anthropic stock, which envisions rapid adoption of Claude and material share gains against rival model builders such as OpenAI, has a fair value of $188, more than twice as high as our base case, implying more than 150% upside to the IPO range midpoint. In our bull case, we model a five-year growth rate of more than 60%, with Anthropic’s share of software and IT services spending growing to 12% by 2031. Bears say: Our bear case, which factors in not only slower enterprise adoption but also robust competition stemming from the open-weight model providers, has a fair value for the stock of $25, implying a 66% downside to the midpoint of the IPO price range. In our bear case, we model growth to be far more moderate, with Anthropic’s five-year growth rate coming in at 22% and the firm’s share of software and IT services spending growing gradually to 3% by 2031. Our Investment Case for Anthropic Stock As part of its IPO documentation, Anthropic has made the development capabilities of its AI models to improve themselves, a process known as recursive self-improvement, a clear part of the investment case for the firm. We are seeing clear progress on this front for the firm. First, Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, now writes more than 90% of contributions to the firm’s codebase. Second, Claude now leads around a quarter of its model research tasks, up from around 1% in March of this year. Third, Anthropic’s amended prospectus claims that the firm’s internal estimates indicate that the firm may soon meet its own threshold for accelerated, AI-driven progress. We have some corroboration of this acceleration, with METR, a safety-focused third-party group that reviewed Anthropic’s internal data, estimating this month that Anthropic’s pace of AI progress has roughly doubled over the past year, with METR attributing loosely 80% of this acceleration to AI itself. While investors may dismiss these claims as dubious or overblown, we are seeing outside AI researchers take them seriously, and we do believe that they merit further attention. Outside AI researchers now see an increasing likelihood that AI can begin outperforming Anthropic’s best human researchers sometime in 2027, which would dramatically accelerate the firm’s product capability unlock and budget capture among enterprises. Implications of Anthropic’s Fast Takeoff Scenario We flag this “fast takeoff” scenario, as it further widens the range of outcomes in both directions. On the upside, if the claims made by outside researchers and METR prove accurate and model improvements generalize beyond certain domains, including coding, then our base case will likely prove far too conservative. We could see an argument that even our bull case, which values the firm’s equity at $3.4 trillion, would be too conservative under a true recursive self-improvement loop scenario. On the downside, however, a misaligned “super AI researcher” may justify an industrywide pause, leading to slowdowns in both model capability improvements and enterprise AI adoption while raising the odds of regulation aimed at slowing frontier AI progress. Computing Consumer Tech Space & Aerospace Earnings Menu Money & Markets Economic Indicators Markets Personal Finance Earnings Menu Lifestyle Cars & Bikes Collecting Entertainment Food & Fine Dining Health and Fitness Real Estate Travel General Trivia Anthropic must pay Alphabet, Nvidia, Microsoft and Amazon whether or not it uses their services The Anthropic IPO filing puts Alphabet, Nvidia, Microsoft and Amazon in focus, as non-cancelable deals commit the AI company to billions in spending with them 1 / 6 List slides Anthropic must pay Alphabet, Nvidia, Microsoft and Amazon whether or not it uses their services List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 9, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz Anthropic has signed multiyear deals that commit it to billions of dollars in spending with some of the largest U.S. technology companies. The payments are owed even if the services go unused. Those commitments are why four tech giants — Alphabet $GOOGL , Nvidia $NVDA , Microsoft $MSFT and Amazon $AMZN — stand to gain as the AI developer moves toward a public listing. Anthropic filed its go-public documents on a Monday and plans to trade under the symbol "ANT." The filing shows $16.3 billion in revenue for the six months ended June 30, a 1,300% increase from the same stretch a year earlier. Losses grew too. The company posted a net loss of $80.7 billion over those six months, up more than 500% from the prior-year period. The documents leave out a listing date, a share count and a price. Investors generally expect the company to carry a market value well above $1 trillion once it does list. The Anthropic IPO is taking shape in a mixed market for technology stocks. The PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 3% over the past week, while the S&P 500 was flat. SpaceX raised more than $85 billion in June in a record IPO. Its shares closed Friday at $147, about 9% above the offering price and about 35% below their intraday high after listing. OpenAI has pushed its own IPO plans to next year. It is raising as much as $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to CNBC. For Alphabet , Nvidia , Microsoft and Amazon , the connection runs through contracts. Several of the four hold multiyear, non-cancelable agreements that lock Anthropic into billions of dollars of spending on their products and services. A public offering would give Anthropic a large new pool of money to draw on as those bills come due. That makes the listing relevant to some of the biggest companies in the S&P 500. Shares of all four also give investors a form of indirect exposure to Anthropic before ANT begins trading. Each slide below covers one company, starting with Alphabet , whose commitment comes with a disclosed dollar figure and timeline. Alphabet's $114.5 billion spending commitment from Anthropic Illustration: Quartz Anthropic has committed to spend at least $114.5 billion on Alphabet $GOOGL 's services between April 2026 and July 2033. If its actual spending comes in below that amount, Anthropic must pay Alphabet the difference. Anthropic agreed to those terms this year. Investopedia gives a dollar figure and a time frame for the Alphabet agreement alone. It describes the arrangements with Nvidia $NVDA , Microsoft $MSFT and Amazon $AMZN only as similar and non-cancelable, with no amounts or periods attached. That makes Alphabet the only one of the four whose contracted minimum from Anthropic is public. The Alphabet agreement works as a spending floor. Anthropic can spend more than $114.5 billion on Alphabet 's services over the period. Spending less does not lower the bill. Any gap between actual use and the minimum becomes a payment to Alphabet . A slowdown in Anthropic's usage would not push what Alphabet receives under the agreement below $114.5 billion. That structure changes the main question for Alphabet . The open issue is not whether Anthropic keeps using the services. It is whether Anthropic can cover the minimum in full. The contract sets the floor, but Alphabet 's receipts still depend on Anthropic meeting the terms it signed. For Alphabet shareholders, the contract puts a number on the company's tie to Anthropic. Alphabet trades under the ticker GOOGL. The $114.5 billion minimum stays in force through July 2033. Anthropic's filing also argues that its compute costs are rising more slowly than its sales. Revenue for the three months ended June rose 1,368% from a year earlier. Compute and infrastructure expenses rose 300% over the same three months, per the filing. Anthropic calls that gap "compute efficiency." Those numbers cover a single quarter, a shorter window than the half-year results reported elsewhere in the filing. In that quarter, each dollar of revenue came with less compute and infrastructure spending than it did a year before. The "compute efficiency" label is Anthropic's own description of that trend. Nvidia's non-cancelable agreement with Anthropic Illustration: Quartz Nvidia $NVDA is one of the tech giants holding a non-cancelable agreement with Anthropic. The AI company owes the committed money whether or not it uses what it signed up for. That arrangement gives NVDA shareholders indirect exposure to Anthropic before ANT shares start trading. The public record on Nvidia 's deal is narrow. Its agreement is described only as similar to the non-cancelable commitments Anthropic made to other large tech companies. No dollar amount, time period or list of covered products has been reported for it. The working relationship between the two companies predates the filing. In November 2025, Nvidia announced that Anthropic would run and scale on Nvidia infrastructure for the first time. Anthropic was to start with one gigawatt of compute capacity on Nvidia 's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems, according to CNBC . That announcement also covered plans for joint engineering and design work. One goal was to tune Anthropic's models for better performance and efficiency. Another was to adapt Nvidia 's architectures to the specific workloads Anthropic runs. Anthropic's go-public filing points to more than one route to Nvidia hardware. CNBC reports that the filing lays out multi-year agreements with SpaceXAI, Nscale and Lambda that give Anthropic a way to obtain Nvidia chips. The filing also lists Nvidia and AMD $AMD graphics processors among the computing resources Anthropic draws on. Those sit alongside AWS Trainium chips from Amazon $AMZN and Google $GOOGL TPUs from Alphabet , two other companies named as beneficiaries of Anthropic's spending. A public offering would give Anthropic a large new pool of funds. For a supplier such as Nvidia , that money supports Anthropic's ability to meet payments that come due regardless of how much it ends up using. Microsoft's multiyear Anthropic deal and what the IPO means for it Illustration: Quartz Microsoft $MSFT has a multiyear, non-cancelable agreement that commits Anthropic to spending on Microsoft 's products and services, according to Investopedia. Anthropic owes that money whether or not it uses what it signed up for. That contract places Microsoft (MSFT) in a group of four tech giants that Investopedia identifies as a route to Anthropic exposure ahead of the listing. Nvidia $NVDA , Amazon $AMZN and Alphabet $GOOGL make up the rest. The outlet describes Microsoft 's agreement as similar to the non-cancelable deals Anthropic holds with those companies. It does not give the deal's dollar value. It does not give the period the commitment covers. It also does not say which Microsoft products and services the agreement includes. Those gaps leave the size of Microsoft 's committed revenue from Anthropic undisclosed. Investors weighing MSFT as a proxy for Anthropic cannot yet measure that commitment against the rest of Microsoft 's business. Without those figures, the strength of Microsoft 's link to Anthropic rests on the contract's structure rather than its size. What is known is that the obligation cannot be canceled and runs for several years. The non-cancelable structure shifts the risk of changing plans onto Anthropic. If the company's needs shrink or move elsewhere, its obligation to Microsoft stays in place. That is where the listing comes in. Money raised from selling shares to the public would add to the cash Anthropic can use to pay what it owes Microsoft . Investopedia counts Microsoft among the biggest S&P 500 companies positioned to benefit from that capital. Infrastructure is one of Anthropic's largest costs. Spending on compute and infrastructure makes up roughly half of what the company spends to operate. In the six months ended June 30, that spending came to $8.9 billion. The reporting does not say how much of that total went to Microsoft . Amazon's committed spending from Anthropic ahead of the ANT listing Illustration: Quartz Amazon $AMZN is one of the four tech giants holding a multiyear, non-cancelable agreement that commits Anthropic to billions of dollars in spending. Anthropic owes Amazon that money even if it does not use the products and services covered by the deal. That contract gives Amazon (AMZN) shareholders indirect exposure to Anthropic before any ANT shares trade. The agreement also includes a shortfall provision. If Anthropic's actual spending with Amazon comes in below the committed amount, the filing requires Anthropic to pay Amazon the difference. That turns the committed amount into a minimum Amazon can expect to collect. That minimum holds even if Anthropic's usage slows. The spending reaches two separate Amazon businesses. Anthropic now buys a large amount of services from both Amazon 's cloud computing unit and its chip operations. The filing lists AWS Trainium among the computing resources Anthropic draws on. The two businesses meet in the way Amazon sells its own silicon. Amazon does not ship Trainium chips to customers as physical products. It sells access to them instead, with the chips running in datacenters that AWS operates. Chip capacity Anthropic buys from Amazon therefore runs inside AWS facilities. Amazon also holds a financial position in Anthropic itself. It owns nonvoting shares in the company. It has neither a seat on Anthropic's board nor an observer seat. That leaves Amazon as both a supplier to Anthropic and one of its shareholders, without a formal role in steering the company. Those are two separate links: one tied to Anthropic's value as a company, the other to its spending on Amazon . A public listing bears directly on the Amazon contract. Money raised in an offering would add to the resources Anthropic can use to keep paying Amazon over the life of the deal, including any shortfall payment. For AMZN holders, that makes the ANT listing a question about how reliably those committed dollars arrive. Meanwhile, the company pays its cloud partners for distribution and has committed to spending hundreds of billions of dollars on their computing capacity. For Anthropic, the three largest cloud providers represent its investors, computing suppliers, sales channels, and competitors all at once. The company explicitly identifies this combination of roles as a source of risk in its prospectus. Details Sales through Google, Amazon, and Microsoft’s cloud marketplaces accounted for 48% of Anthropic’s revenue in the first half of 2026, versus 11% in 2023, according to the company’s prospectus, published on Monday. The cloud providers bill Anthropic’s customers and pass along their payments after deducting fees. In the first half, fees paid to channel partners, a group that includes the cloud providers, rose $2.7 billion year over year. Cloud sales have helped fuel Anthropic’s rapid growth, Bloomberg notes . Second-quarter revenue reached $11.6 billion, while operating profit totaled $974 million. At the same time, Anthropic disclosed massive computing purchase commitments in its prospectus: at least $114.5 billion to Google through 2033, $110 billion to Amazon through 2036, and $44.9 billion to Microsoft. In addition, the management estimates that payments for additional computing capacity based on Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), supplied by Google and other providers and scheduled for delivery in 2028-2031, will total $125-150 billion. What are the risks for Anthropic? In its IPO filing, Anthropic describes the cloud providers as “investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors” simultaneously. Anthropic warns that these companies have access to information about its pricing and commercial terms and could favor their own AI models. Its relationships with them have also attracted antitrust scrutiny and could draw more in the future. Moving workloads to other providers would be “costly, time-consuming” and could reduce its compute efficiency, Anthropic acknowledged. Anthropic has previously been criticized for participating in “circular deals” in the tech ecosystem, with the same companies both putting money into its balance sheet and taking it out, Bloomberg writes. For example, Anthropic is a major Amazon Web Services customer, using Amazon’s data centers and chips to train and run its Claude models, while Amazon offers Claude through its Bedrock platform. Similarly, Anthropic uses Google’s custom AI chips, while Google sells Claude through its own cloud platform. Amazon and Google are among Anthropic’s largest shareholders. After the conversion of preferred shares and certain debt instruments in connection with the IPO, each company will own more than 5% of Anthropic, according to the prospectus. Their shares, however, carry no voting rights. Amazon has invested about $18 billion in Anthropic since 2023 and committed up to another $15 billion, subject to certain conditions. Convertible debt instruments could also give Amazon an additional stake of up to 10.9% on a fully diluted basis as of June, excluding the shares it already owns. Amazon’s stake is capped at 12% unless it waives that limit. Google has invested about $23 billion in Anthropic and committed another $20 billion tied to performance targets. Its stake is capped at 14.99%, though Google can also waive that limit. Anthropic’s IPO will test public market investors’ appetite for an AI business amid growing concerns about massive infrastructure spending, Bloomberg writes. The company’s third-quarter revenue growth disappointed Wall Street and intensified the tech selloff amid concerns that AI investment is outpacing demand. He says quiet AI skeptics won't become top performers where coworkers use agents. He says Shopify's AI expectations now happen organically, without him having to enforce them. Shopify's performance reviews asked how staff used AI. Its CEO says the answers didn't matter, and the question can give a company a reputation to live up to. SEJ STAFF Matt G. Southern October 31, 2026 ⋅ 4 min read SEJ STAFF Matt G. Southern Senior News Writer at Search Engine Journal Bio Follow 552 READS Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke says it didn’t matter how employees answered the AI question his company added to its performance reviews. Having the question there, he said on the Sources podcast , can “give a company a reputation to live up to.” The question came out of an April 2025 memo in which he told employees “reflexive AI usage is now a baseline expectation at Shopify.” The memo said, “We will add AI usage questions to our performance and peer review questionnaire.” It also said teams would have to show why AI couldn’t do the work before asking for more headcount and resources. He made the comments to Alex Heath in an episode published Oct. 28 and recorded at Shopify’s Toronto office. He also said an AI skeptic who keeps their head down won’t become a top performer at a company where everyone around them works with AI agents. Shopify’s 2025 AI Rules, A Year And A Half Later Heath asked whether Shopify still had the AI review question and the headcount rule in place. Lütke said both now happen on their own. “I don’t have to enforce these kind of things,” he said. He said the memo was seen as controversial outside Shopify but “really not inside of a firm.” More people there paid attention to it, he said, after the press “made a big deal out of it.” He took that as a sign Shopify had already made the transition. He said he doesn’t know whether the AI question is in Shopify’s current review. He described it as a peer-rating question about how reflexively a colleague shows up with an AI prototype, and said “sometimes you play a little bit of tricks there.” The answer didn’t matter, he said. AI Skeptics And Top Performers Shopify’s CEO moved from the review question to people who resist AI. He pointed to open-source projects that have banned AI contributions and said he’s entertained by debates over whether code was “hand chiseled by humans or somehow computed by math.” His view was that good code should be accepted either way. He said a company should decide who it’s for and who it isn’t, and that “heightening the misalignment with the people you don’t want is actually almost more important than having a good careers page.” An AI skeptic who is “just kind of trying to lay low,” he said, will never be a top performer in a company where everyone around them uses AI agents to do their work. He said companies should make that explicit, because everyone deserves to work somewhere they “either are or have a really good shot at becoming one of the top performers.” Once it’s clear that isn’t possible for someone, Shopify also wants to help them look for that kind of place elsewhere, he said. His September Comments On ‘Slop Grenades’ In a Knowledge Project episode released Sept. 15, Lütke said AI had made one kind of lazy work worse at Shopify. Staff have a name for AI output that gets handed to a colleague without being read. They call it a slop grenade, and I covered those comments last month. Why This Matters Shopify’s CEO says the AI question in its reviews was there to give the company a reputation to live up to. The question he described is about how readily someone turns to AI. The slop grenades he talked about in September come after that, when AI output reaches a coworker unread. A review question about adoption won’t tell a team lead whether anyone checks AI drafts before they go to an editor or a client. Looking Ahead Earlier in the interview, Shopify’s CEO said he doesn’t expect public pessimism about AI to last long, because more people will use it themselves. He said the stories from that use will wash it away. He didn’t say in the interview whether the AI question will be in Shopify’s next review cycle. Across the country, Democrats scored victories in GOP strongholds, flipping at least seven Senate seats and winning House races in districts Republicans easily carried in 2024. Several news organizations projected that Democrats would win the House, while Decision Desk HQ projected they took the Senate. I have no doubt that Iran and the economy played significant roles in this election; what stood out to me, however, was very much Stratechery fodder. Specifically, I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite. Meanwhile in Texas, from Yahoo Finance : A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state’s first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies. The state is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers…Hinojosa, Texas’ first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030. Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, I would note, already declared a moratorium on new data-center permits in September; that’s how much of a hot-button issue this is, including in the state that is the biggest opportunity and beneficiary of the data center buildout. So yeah, this is a Stratechery topic of concern. The Data Center Veto Earlier this year, while writing about data center opposition , I said: There really wasn’t widespread opposition to data centers when they were being built for the Internet generally; indeed, local governments would compete for them, eager for the economic benefits that came during their construction and the long-term tax benefits once they were operational. In other words, it seems pretty clear that the current wave of opposition can’t be divorced from AI — you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race. I do not, I don’t think, need to explain to you why this is not a very compelling message, and, in the very long run, I do think that humans will have economic value . At the same time, it’s hard to explain the huge amount of investment that is going into AI, not just at the model level but also in terms of data centers, without admitting that a big part of the thesis is that AI can not just increase the top line for companies, but also increase the bottom line — i.e. replace the jobs of some number of humans. Again, I’m generally an optimist here, but this already happened with the first wave of IT . That leads to an interesting contrast to globalization: when companies were closing down American factories and laying off workers and moving operations to China, none of the affected towns or workers had a say. They just suddenly no longer had a job, and a huge number of cities across the Rust Belt no longer had a reason to exist. People simply had to move, or worse, retreat to things like alcohol or drugs. AI, however, is the opposite: building data centers requires permission, which is to say that people actually have a say. Again, I am not at all saying that these people are well informed about data centers, or about the economic impact on their communities, much less the economic impact of AI generally; what I am noting is that people who didn’t have a say in globalization are suddenly finding they do have a say about AI, and it’s not a surprise they are expressing their disapproval by blocking data centers. That message was loud and clear last spring; now it is deafening, and it’s tempting to say that tech, particularly the frontier labs, have no one to blame but themselves. In fact, however, some of the biggest culprits may, in the long run, be some of the biggest beneficiaries of the anti-data center wave. My thesis — driven not just by national results and the Texas governorship, but also the fact that, as this thread documents , nearly every relevant local ballot measure opposing data centers won or is winning ( the only exception so far was in North Dakota ) — is that the constraint on AI dispersion has shifted once again. First we were short on compute, but that ramped; now we are short on memory, but that will ramp; we were coming close to being short on power, but that will be rectified. The final constraint is political, and that may be the most imposing constraint of all. Not only is it harder to solve, but it actually interferes with solving the other constraints. Many of the theories about AI assume that it becomes a commodity; I think it’s just as likely we are looking at scarcity for much longer than we expected, which will have ripple effects on everything. Ten Takes To that end, here — with the caveat that nothing leads to hot takes you regret like an election — are ten perspectives on what a permanently impaired ability to build might mean. To be clear, I’m not declaring permanency — look at how our elections swing back and forth — but it’s worth considering what the implications might be if Americans don’t change their minds about data centers. 1. The AI Trade Got It Right The most obvious reason why the stock market has been rocky over the last few weeks is the tightening of credit markets, which I wrote about this summer . We are, needless to say, full on into the equity funding era (and while I’m here, I haven’t written about Anthropic’s updated S-1 , but it strongly affirms my initial analysis ). At the same time, it seems clear that this outcome is very bad for the AI trade in the short term, but much of the pain may have already been endured. 2. Neoclouds on the Edge The Neoclouds have been at the forefront of credit concerns, and from a certain perspective, being unable to build data centers has a silver lining in that they couldn’t get the money to pay for them anyways. Moreover, Neoclouds with facilities that are already permitted now have an asset that is going to be scarcer than expected. At the same time, it’s Neoclouds that need new sites and new permits, even as they are likely to have much less political sway than the hyperscalers — who already have more sites they can repurpose or rebuild. It was already getting harder to get capital, relative to the hyperscalers; now you have to layer on that it’s going to be harder to get permission, too. 3. Hyperscalers Are Winners The downside for the neoclouds is upside for the hyperscalers, who are more likely to grow their share of AI compute than they were before. Moreover, investors may be pleased if the hyperscalers’ ambitions are somewhat curtailed; political opposition is an excuse to moderate spending, knowing that everyone else is in the same boat. 4. Nvidia’s Mixed Bag Nvidia will almost certainly be a short-term loser. Fewer data centers mean fewer Nvidia chips generally, and a weakened Neocloud set is particularly harmful not only because Neoclouds almost exclusively use Nvidia full-rack systems, but also because Nvidia is back-stopping a huge number of them. It’s the hyperscalers, meanwhile, who are Nvidia’s biggest long-term threat, given their scale and ability to invest in their own chips. At the same time, a constrained world makes Nvidia’s offerings more compelling. CEO Jensen Huang actually spent an entire keynote making this point back in 2025; I wrote in an Update : When Huang says “iso power” he means that power is the constraint; the question is how many tokens can you generate given a fixed power envelope, and Blackwell can generate a lot more. These were the numbers Huang gave for a 100 MW data center: What this means is that the first order of business for an ASIC maker is to match that level of efficiency. That, though, means keeping up with Nvidia’s product development cadence; The Information has a post about Amazon offering instances using its latest Trainium ASIC at a significant discount to the H100. Huang, though, spent this keynote insulting the H100! You can almost hear him speaking to Amazon directly: you spent all this money, and are offering these huge discounts, just to entice developers to lock themselves into an inferior chip, even as reasoning models are going to swamp your available power generation… Huang is issuing a challenge to every cloud provider tempted to make an ASIC: do you really think that you can keep up with this, and risk running out of power capacity because your chips aren’t efficient enough? Don’t even try. A world without power or data center constraints is one where it is, in the very long run, very difficult to maintain Nvidia’s margins; once those constraints start to bite, however, an advantage in tokens/megawatt is worth a lot of money. Go back to my point about the hyperscalers: one way to generate more tokens is to build a new data center; another way is to rebuild a data center with new Nvidia chips. 5. Advantage China China is the inverse of the scenario that Huang laid out: the country has plenty of power and the ability to build a lot more, but they don’t have leading-edge chips. Some of the advantages of leading-edge chips, however, can be overcome by simply throwing tons of electricity at the problem. From a 2025 Update about the Huawei CloudMatrix 384 supercomputer: The CloudMatrix 384, which is a supercomputer consisting of 384 chips, takes up dramatically more space, uses dramatically more power, is almost certainly dramatically more expensive to make, and is dramatically more brittle than Nvidia’s NVL72; there is no one in the world who would choose the CloudMatrix 384 over the NVL72 if they had the choice. That’s the thing, though: China doesn’t have the choice, because of U.S. export controls. The country’s saving grace is that they are operating on different constraints than the U.S.…China — which actually builds power generation — is not iso power; they are iso compute: Huawei’s goal with the CloudMatrix 384 is to get as much compute as possible, power efficiency be damned. In the fullness of time — i.e. as China figures out leading-edge chips — this may be an insurmountable advantage. 6. Data Centers in Space When SpaceX released their S-1, I explicitly pointed to political opposition to data centers as one of the company’s most significant upside scenarios: The third question about data centers in space is if there is a stick. Specifically, while I think that racks-in-space are both a lot more viable than people think, and a lot more relevant to agentic inference than current modes of compute, it is at the end of the day cheaper and easier to build on earth, all things being equal. All things are not equal, however: right now we are at the very beginning of the AI buildout and already one of the biggest constraints is not just power (expected), but zoning (unexpected). I wrote in an Update last week: I already posted the relevant excerpt above. Continuing: In that Update I made the case that data center builders — and by extension the companies that use them — should straight up pay people for permission to build data centers in their communities. At a minimum, however, that increases the costs of terrestrial data centers. What seems very plausible in the long run is that the demand for compute ends up being so large that there eventually is nowhere left to build, making the vast expanses of space not just an alternative but in fact the only choice. This is where I come back to my experience watching these campaign ads: this isn’t a partisan issue, where the pendulum will swing back in two years. Both parties see opposition to data centers as a winning cause, and not just nationally: that thread has multiple examples of local officials straight up recalled for approving data centers in their localities. Space will be incredibly difficult, but difficulty is all relative! Moreover, to the extent opposition is permanent, the more this actually reduces the risk of data centers in space, because investors will have more confidence in there being enduring demand. 7. The Frontier Labs Benefit If the hyperscalers had a red queen problem , the frontier labs have it even worse: the biggest revelation from Anthropic’s S-1 was that their inference margins were very high (good!), which meant that their massive compute costs were actually in R&D; this is bad because that R&D spend is governed by competition with the other frontier labs, and absent constraints, that spend looked set to surpass revenue sooner rather than later. Now, however, it is the public that is effectively demanding that the frontier be paced, which is great for the frontier labs’ financial outlook. The upside goes further than that: the point about efficiency being more important in a world of constraints doesn’t just matter for chips, but also for models. Devoting limited compute to inefficient and costlier-to-serve Chinese models is a poor trade if there isn’t enough compute. Moreover, open models may be at greater regulatory risk, as Democrats seem much more likely to pass laws that ultimately favor the frontier labs. There are some counter-arguments. First, if compute is constrained, and thus more expensive, then that will increase the drive to right-size models for jobs, which is a big argument in favor of open models; the fact that compute won’t be a commodity means that the frontier labs’ lower cost to serve will never come to bear on the low end of the market. And, it’s worth noting, it will be harder for the frontier labs to build their own compute, leaving them dependent on the hyperscalers; big tech wins again. 8. Apple Gains The most obvious advantage for Apple is that in a world of constrained compute, inference on the edge will be that much more important. Another advantage is that any slowdown in the dispersion of AI is good for a company that dominated the previous paradigm . The biggest advantage of all, however, is that any slowdown in the AI buildout offers hope that the memory crunch will ease. This will take a while, to be sure, but no company would be a bigger beneficiary of the world running out of places to put AI chips than Apple. 9. Startups Suffer AI has drawn a great many battle lines, not just in terms of data centers, but also within AI, and between AI and the rest of tech. Specifically, anything that strengthens the frontier labs is likely bad for the rest of the startup ecosystem. In a world with fewer data centers, startups will have less access to cheap compute, even as a slowdown in capabilities both means it takes longer to build compelling products and also gives the frontier labs time to actually build products that secure their ownership of the end user. 10. The Human Factor One major fear that investors have had about the data center buildout is that there would be too much capacity, causing prices to plummet and investors and creditors to lose their shirts; that scenario, however, would be great for users, who would suddenly have access to incredibly cheap compute. Of course most users aren’t going to use AI directly; what they will miss out on is the equivalent of the Web 2.0 wave of free Internet services that were predicated on compute being free. Now there’s a good chance that AI is going to have meaningful marginal costs for a long time to come. At the same time, while I have been an optimist about humans in an AI future , there is no question that we were and are facing a wrenching change as intelligence becomes a commodity. It follows, however, that if it doesn’t become a commodity — or if that change takes longer than expected — that humanity will have more time to adapt. Maybe this is a break we needed; what is increasingly clear is it’s the break Americans wanted. That noted, there is a long history of citizens demanding the ends and opposing the means, and it’s the demand that wins in the end. The big difference today is that, unlike the first few waves of tech, the industry is going to need to do some convincing, and break the habit of assuming everything it does will get the benefit of the doubt. AI wasn’t technically on the ballot, but it was implicitly, and will be forevermore. Presented by I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. What I often find I’m missing is a view across the economy itself. With more than 1.7% of global GDP running on Stripe, working with them means I can bring some of what they’re seeing to Stratechery. They are, in a sense, a barometer of the economy. Take the “SaaSpocalypse”. Earlier this year, nearly a trillion dollars in enterprise software value disappeared amid fears of AI eating its lunch. Stock prices only tell us what investors think will happen, and not necessarily what is happening. In this case, Stripe recently built a SaaS Index using payments data from 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses. Looking at their actual performance, we can see that while SaaS stocks were selling off, revenue growth was actually accelerating. Year-over-year growth is now over 30%, with some of the fastest growth coming from the youngest SaaS companies. I suspect there are a lot more interesting things hiding in Stripe’s data, and I’m excited about having an excuse to go look for them. sources.title: Welcome to the B2A Economy | Andreessen Horowitz
sources.relevance: Provides broader context for the environmental melt facing companies: internet systems increasingly need to serve autonomous agents as customers and economic actors, not merely humans.
sources.claim: Companies that once designed systems to exclude bots are beginning to compete for autonomous agents’ business.
sources.excerpt: Companies spent decades keeping bots out. Now they’ll compete for their business.
sources.content_text: Portfolio Team Focus Areas Focus Areas AI American Dynamism Bio + Health Consumer Cultural Leadership Fund Enterprise Fintech Frontier Growth Infrastructure Perennial Speedrun Content Content News & Content News & Content The Latest General new Super Intelligence-Era Critical Infrastructure Cyber Defense Plan Anne Neuberger Consumer new Gaming’s Next Origin Stories Elena Burger, Anish Acharya, and Jonathan Lai Infra new Investing in General Translation Jennifer Li, Martin Casado, and Jason Cui Consumer new Welcome to the B2A Economy Olivia Moore and Justine Moore Newsletters Podcast Network New Media Books Programs Programs a16z Build College Talent Company Company About Jobs Offices a16z Global Strategic Partnerships Twitter Linkedin Facebook Instagram Youtube-alt Substack Close Consumer Welcome to the B2A Economy Olivia Moore and Justine Moore Posted November 10, 2026 Subscribe Share Share Email X LinkedIn Facebook Hacker News WhatsApp Flipboard Reddit Share Share Email X LinkedIn Facebook Hacker News WhatsApp Flipboard Reddit The primary users of the Internet are no longer human. They’re AI agents. Agents now make up the majority of web traffic, write more than half of new articles published online, and generate most of the code pushed to production. This is what the early stage of a platform shift looks like: adoption is measurable, but the business models it enables mostly aren’t visible yet. Every prior shift changed both what people could do and how businesses reached them. The Web gave businesses a storefront anyone could visit; mobile put that storefront in everyone’s pocket. AI has already changed what people can do, but its transformation of distribution is just beginning. As agents move from answering questions to completing tasks, they’ll increasingly decide which products to use, which services to subscribe to, and where to spend money on our behalf. Businesses that treat agents as first-class customers have a shot at a wave of growth. Those that don’t may find themselves under threat. For years, retailers and platforms built walls to keep bots out – now, they will have to fight for bots’ business. If agents break out to the true consumer and capture real usage, they’ll unlock the biggest unrealized opportunity in AI: a true platform shift. Every prior platform shift (web, mobile) paired a new product capability with a new distribution mechanism. AI has overperformed on the first and underperformed on the second, which is a big reason consumer adoption has stayed so limited outside ChatGPT. The early signs of a distribution shift are already here. LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok are a large and valuable source of traffic for many businesses. Shopify reported that AI-driven traffic to its stores grew eightfold year over year in Q1 ‘26, while orders from AI-powered searches grew nearly thirteenfold. And it’s accelerating: Human Security saw agentic browser traffic grow 8x between August and October, with Muse driving the largest share of activity (60%) and OpenAI products reaching a combined 30%. Just like websites could target users more effectively than billboards, agents should hypothetically be an even stronger referral source – as they have deep and specific data on the user and their needs. So far, this is proving to be true – AI-referred consumer traffic is higher engagement and converts better to revenue than non-AI traffic, with a lower bounce rate. Even pre-agents, an estimated 11% of shopper journeys in the U.S. visited AI before a transactional site. Right now, most of this traffic is happening via browser use – where an agent either takes over the user’s browser, or spins up its own virtual machine and browser instance, and completes the task by clicking around like a human would. However, we’re starting to see the emergence of the equivalent of an App Store for agents, but on steroids – connectors, plug-ins, and MCPs, where agents can more directly access third-party tools and sites. As one example – we asked ChatGPT to create and edit a video ad using the Krea, Descript, and Eleven Labs plug-ins. It coordinated across the products, and upsold us on a Descript paid plan to get the video done. Using an agent to sign up or pay for a product will only get easier as the underlying platforms allow a user to “lend” their identity or tokens to other products to get a task done (ex. Sign in with ChatGPT ). Eventually, agents will be able to select and install the tools they need without human intervention – Claude already allows enterprise admins to connect plugins for their entire organization. Just yesterday, OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT – companies can now claim their business, add product feeds, and see insights on how users interact with them on ChatGPT. There are a few categories of companies that may stand to benefit from the B2A economy: Agents / agentic models – most people picture ‘consumer agents’ as standalone harnesses like Instinct, Muse, and Wabi. We believe every product will soon operate agentically, as the models behind them get more action-oriented. ChatGPT (with 1.2 billion weekly active users) has a particularly intriguing opportunity here. Products newly enabled by agents – Amazon needed the Internet to come to life, and Uber could not have existed without the mobile phone. We expect agents to produce their own examples. Exactly how is hard to predict, but a few themes include self-running SMBs, marketplaces or network products that are AI-intermediated, and auto-optimizers. Incumbents who optimize for agents – LLMs have already been a significant source of traffic for many websites, which formed the basis of the generative engine optimization (GEO) industry. GEO largely stops at discovery. Agents will take it further, into evaluation and execution of purchase / signup choices, an even larger market. Agent infrastructure – for agents to operate in the real world on behalf of their humans, they’ll need their own set of tools. We’re already seeing system strain at fairly low agent volume on payments, fraud and identity, and communication (iMessage, calls, email, etc.). We already have one case study of how this might play out – coding agents, which completely transformed developer behavior. As of September 2026, upwards of 40% of GitHub PRs started with an agent’s draft – versus just 17% six months prior. Like consumer agents, coding agents have to rely on external tools to complete tasks. Say a user asks an agent to build a website. Finishing that job may require a database, hosting, authentication, email delivery, and monitoring. Beyond the agentic models and harnesses themselves (Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, Cognition, as well as vibe coding platforms like Replit, Lovable, and Base44), many other players saw growth: Supabase reported in June ‘26 that more than 60% of new databases are launched by AI tools Neon reported in May ‘25 that automated agents deploy 80% of its new databases Stripe reported in June ‘26 that agents accounted for nearly 40% of documentation traffic and 70% of CLI requests for API resources Vercel reported in October ‘26 that agent-triggered deployments had increased 28x over the last twelve months Fewer than 1% of the global workforce is developers – what happens when the other 99% starts using agents? This is the first in a series of pieces exploring the agent economy. Calling it “AI commerce” undersells the opportunity – yes, agents will drive transaction volume to physical products and services. But, they will also reshape how traffic, tokens, and revenue are routed to digital products. Most enterprises are still blocking agent traffic due to concerns about fraud and chargebacks, but we believe they’ll have to embrace an increasingly valuable wave. Over the next few weeks, we’ll be publishing more insights and data around what consumer agent usage looks like now, how agents are deciding which sites and products to direct traffic to, how infrastructure is developing around agents, and what the remaining hurdles are for agents to complete transactions. This space is changing on a daily basis – below is our best current mapping of the market. This includes the agents themselves, as well as the infrastructure that allows them to exist.   About the Contributors Olivia Moore X Linkedin is a partner on the investing team at Andreessen Horowitz, where she focuses on AI. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Jensen Huang Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after alleged affairs Move follows admission of affair with woman alleged to be Chinese spy and reported relationships with two employees Nvidia crisis – live updates From washing dishes at Denny’s to rockstar of AI: the rise and fall of Jensen Huang Dan Milmo and Dara Kerr Thu 12 Nov 2026 17.05 EST First published on Thu 12 Nov 2026 09.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jensen Huang has resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two company employees. He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a full-time successor is named. Shares in the chipmaker plunged by 13% when Wall Street opened, after Huang’s departure was announced. After a partial rebound, they closed down 4.3% on Thursday, wiping more than $180bn (£135bn) off Nvidia’s value on the day and around $490bn for the week – valuing the company at $4tn. The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded. “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the statement said. It added that Huang had resigned as chief executive, president and Nvidia board member “effective immediately”. A graphic showing Nvidia’s share price fluctuating over time Donald Trump, who had defended Huang at first as the scandal threatened to overwhelm the Nvidia co-founder, quickly moved on to potential successors on Thursday, posting on social media that he should be replaced by Tim Cook, Apple’s former chief executive and current executive chair. “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote, adding: “A Legend replaces a Legend!” The chipmaker’s board earlier this week appointed the leading law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship with Alice Huang, an Nvidia customer and Chinese citizen who is no relation to the Nvidia boss. Nvidia had previously denied anything unusual about the relationship, but that changed on Sunday when Jensen Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, Lori, without referring to Alice Huang directly. The law firm had directed Jensen Huang to continue to lead Nvidia as the investigation continued. However, late on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee named Kimberly Powell. She was Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March. The report added to the pressure on Huang, as the board called a meeting late on Wednesday to discuss the chief executive’s future. Powell has been approached for comment. After Huang’s resignation was announced on Thursday, Reuters reported a third alleged affair. The newly uncovered liaison was another Nvidia employee, according to two people familiar with the matter who spoke to the news outlet. Reuters did not reveal her name. Nvidia’s board said it would consider internal and external candidates for the chief executive’s role, with Cook featuring among potential runners and riders before Trump’s intervention. Cook stepped down as chief executive at Apple in September but still has a senior executive role at the company. Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker, has also been mooted, along with Lisa Su, the chief executive of the chipmaker AMD. Huang ran Nvidia tightly and managed about 60 direct reports. Internal candidates include Kress and Ian Buck, who manages the company’s AI hardware and software products. Huang’s two children, Madison and Spencer, also work at Nvidia but are in their mid-30s and relatively inexperienced. The chipmaker also announced the appointment of Harvey Jones, a tech investor and entrepreneur, as its first-ever chair. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion Dan Ives, a senior US tech analyst, said the board had done what “it needed to do, which is rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him” and that the company remained ahead of its competitors. However, Neil Wilson, an analyst at the investment platform Saxo UK, said Nvidia would need a “great CEO” to replace Huang. “His technical knowledge and understanding of every last bit of product is basically unique and impossible to replicate,” Wilson said, adding nonetheless that Nvidia was well placed in terms of upcoming products and orders. Huang’s exit from the company he co-founded in 1993 removes a senior figure in Silicon Valley at a time when the AI arms race between the US and China is at an apex. He owns more than 870m shares, or about 3.6% of the company, and was worth $145bn on Thursday morning, according to Bloomberg, making him the world’s 13th richest person. Unlike many of his contemporaries at other leading tech companies, Huang has dozens of direct reports, an unusual management structure that emphasises his control over the company. The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. It is also one of the most valuable companies on Earth, with a market cap that hit $5tn at one point last year. Huang has denied any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years. Alice Huang is a businesswoman and head of the Singapore-based datacentre firm Megaspeed, who US intelligence services suspect of being a Chinese asset according to multiple reports. On the same day that Jensen Huang admitted having an affair, Nvidia’s board of directors announced the company was launching an investigation regarding reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has agreed to testify before US Congress. Anthropic said the shared computing pool would allow resources to be directed towards frontier research, model development, customer demand and internal use of Claude, depending on workload requirements and price-performance considerations. According to CNBC, the Anthropic IPO now faces a market that is auditing every dollar of AI spending, just days after the company filed a prospectus showing $16.3 billion in first-half revenue and an $80.7 billion net loss. Table of Contents What Changed for the Anthropic IPO This Week The S-1 Numbers Behind the Anthropic IPO Why the $80.7B Loss Is Not the Whole Story The efficiency figure bulls will quote Big Tech AI Spending Cuts Into Free Cash Flow The Compute Bill Anthropic Has Already Signed The Valuation Reset From $2 Trillion to $1.5 Trillion Market Backdrop: Nasdaq Slump and a Narrowing IPO Window Customer Concentration and Cloud Marketplace Reliance Risk Factors: 94 Pages Investors Are Reading Control and governance How the Three Cloud Partners Compare as Backers Historical Context: When AI Funding Windows Narrow Five Predictions for the Anthropic IPO What Developers and Enterprise Buyers Should Watch Frequently Asked Questions When is the Anthropic IPO expected? How much did Anthropic lose in the first half of 2026? What is Anthropic’s IPO valuation? Why does Big Tech AI spending affect the Anthropic IPO? How much has Anthropic committed to spend on compute? Is Anthropic profitable? Who controls Anthropic after the IPO? Related Coverage The timing hurts. Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon all reported quarterly results after the filing landed, and the numbers pushed investors to ask whether the data center buildout can pay for itself. Our earlier breakdown of the five big questions in the Anthropic S-1 covers the filing itself. This piece focuses on what changed since, and what it means for the offering. Reports say valuation discussions have fallen from an earlier, higher range, which frames the debate for the rest of the month. Below, we lay out the numbers, the partners, the risks and five predictions. The Shattered Newsletter The week's biggest stories in tech, gaming and security, in one email. Add now What Changed for the Anthropic IPO This Week Anthropic, PBC filed its Form S-1 on October 26, 2026, and followed with a roadshow launched on November 10, 2026 for 825 million Class A shares at an expected $70–$78 per share. The company plans to list Class A shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading a 22-bank underwriting group, according to reports summarizing the filing. Fortune reported that the listing is expected during Thanksgiving week. Three things hit the story after that. First, the hyperscalers that supply Anthropic’s computing capacity reported earnings, and two of the three posted negative free cash flow. Second, the Nasdaq Composite posted its first three-week losing streak since March, per CNBC. Third, other companies pulled or postponed their own IPOs, which narrowed the window Anthropic wanted. You may like Anthropic IPO Valuation Slips to $1.2T Floor [2026] Anthropic IPO and Nvidia Earnings: $64.4B, $109B Test Anthropic IPO Mirrors SpaceX: 28% Passive Demand [2026] Bloomberg framed the core test plainly: Anthropic must convince investors that revenue will outrun computing costs. Forbes ran a piece arguing the offering may be ill-timed even though the company leans into profitability. Benzinga reported that Blackstone sounded a warning about AI bubble risk. Each outlet reached for the same tension between growth and capital intensity. None of this means the deal is off. Nothing in the reporting says Anthropic has pulled or delayed its filing, and the company went ahead with the roadshow it launched on November 10, 2026. It does mean the pricing conversation moved from how high to how defensible. The S-1 Numbers Behind the Anthropic IPO The prospectus is a strange document. It shows a business that grew 1,300% in six months, and a headline loss larger than most companies will ever book. Fortune pulled out the figures that matter most, and CNBC added several more. Metric Figure Source H1 2026 revenue $16.3 billion Fortune Revenue growth, first half 1,300% Fortune, CNBC H1 2026 net loss $80.7 billion Fortune Non-cash convertible note charge $72.4 billion Fortune H1 2026 operating loss $693 million (vs. $2.1 billion a year earlier) Fortune Adjusted operating income $1.6 billion (about 10% margin) Fortune Operating cash flow, H1 +$3.9 billion (vs. -$1.5 billion a year earlier) Fortune Implied gross margin 85% CNBC Net revenue retention 900% CNBC Employees, end of September 5,300 Fortune Read the table top to bottom and the story splits in two. The loss line looks catastrophic, yet the operating line shows a business that shrank its operating loss to $693 million while revenue exploded. Cash flow turned positive. That is the case the bankers will make on the road show. Why the $80.7B Loss Is Not the Whole Story Most of the headline loss is accounting. Fortune reported that $72.4 billion of the $80.7 billion came from non-cash fair-value changes on convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs. Strip that out and the remaining loss is far smaller, and the operating loss sits below $700 million. Fortune’s second piece went further, arguing that investors will likely look past the $81 billion hole. The logic is simple. Fair-value charges rise when a company’s valuation rises, so a bigger loss on those instruments partly reflects a higher price tag. Public investors usually care about operating trends and cash. The efficiency figure bulls will quote The S-1 gives one number that bulls will repeat constantly. Per Fortune, Anthropic spent $5.6 billion on compute in the second quarter and booked $11.6 billion in revenue, or $2.08 of revenue per compute dollar. If that ratio holds as volumes climb, the business model works. If it slips as the company chases larger customers with discounts, the bear case gets teeth. The earlier filing coverage on this site, including our look at how shaky partners complicate the $80.7B loss , flagged the same dependency. The company’s economics are good only if somebody else’s data centers show up on time. Big Tech AI Spending Cuts Into Free Cash Flow The hyperscaler results turned an Anthropic story into a sector story. CNBC compiled the three cloud giants’ numbers, and the contrast is sharp. Microsoft still generates cash. Alphabet and Amazon do not, at least not right now. Company Capex outlook (per CNBC) Free cash flow (per CNBC) Other signal Microsoft (Q1 FY2027) Capex forecast trimmed to $170 billion from $175 billion $18.6 billion $25 billion bond offering, cloud growth beat estimates Alphabet (Q3 2026) Guidance up to $205 billion Negative $9.1 billion Cloud revenue more than doubled, stock fell nearly 13% in a day Amazon (Q3 2026) Roughly $220 billion Negative $42.4 billion (trailing 12 months) Second straight quarter of negative free cash flow, cloud growth beat estimates Add up the three capex figures and you get about $595 billion in planned spending. That total is our arithmetic on CNBC’s numbers, and the three companies guide on different fiscal calendars, so treat it as a rough scale marker rather than a precise sum. Our analysis of Big Tech’s cash burn reached a similar conclusion about the direction of travel. Amazon’s case drew the sharpest attention. We covered the negative $42.4 billion free cash flow figure the day it hit. Cloud growth beat estimates there, and still the stock reaction was harsh, which tells you what investors prioritize right now. The Compute Bill Anthropic Has Already Signed Anthropic’s own commitments explain why hyperscaler cash flow matters to its IPO. According to reports on the prospectus, the company plans to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon for cloud services through April 2036. It also plans $120 billion with SpaceX through 2029, $115 billion with Google and $45 billion with Microsoft, the last two through 2033. Partner Planned spend Through Amazon At least $110 billion April 2036 SpaceX $120 billion 2029 Google $115 billion 2033 Microsoft $45 billion 2033 Four named partners combined At least $390 billion (our sum) Varies The $390 billion total is our addition of the four reported figures. Other commitments may exist, since CNBC described hundreds of billions of dollars in compute commitments overall. Reading the table, two things stand out. The SpaceX deal has the shortest runway, so it carries the steepest annual payments. And three of the four partners are also Anthropic’s biggest sales channels, which creates a loop where cloud spending and cloud revenue feed each other. Investors have a name for that loop: circular financing. Coverage of the IPO market this week described investors auditing the mechanics of debt-fueled circular financing, along with AI capital spending returns and steep valuations. Anthropic did not invent the structure, but its prospectus makes the structure unusually visible. The Valuation Reset From $2 Trillion to $1.5 Trillion The valuation picture shifted fast. Reports said some current and prospective investors valued Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion, versus roughly $2 trillion a week earlier, after the company disclosed financial details at an investor event, and a report dated November 13, 2026 reportedly put valuation discussions lower still, at approximately $1.1 trillion–$1.3 trillion. Fortune separately reported a targeted range of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, with one prediction that the stock could reach $2.4 trillion after listing. Those figures conflict, and the conflict is the point. Nobody outside the syndicate knows the final range, and the price will move with the Nasdaq between now and pricing. An analyst who says $2.4 trillion and a fund that says $1.5 trillion are describing a spread of $900 billion, which is wider than most public companies are worth. Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group, told CNBC that the market sees more doubt around capital structure, and he also called the prospectus very impressive. That pairing sums up the mood. Analysts admire the growth, and they question who funds it. A lower private mark does not automatically hurt the IPO. A cheaper entry price can attract buyers who skipped the earlier rounds. The risk is momentum. If the first weeks of trading disappoint, a $1.5 trillion valuation could look like a ceiling instead of a floor. Market Backdrop: Nasdaq Slump and a Narrowing IPO Window The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.9% on Friday, its first three-week losing streak since March, according to CNBC. Intel issued a weak forecast and suffered its steepest one-day drop since the 1970s. Alphabet dropped nearly 13% on Thursday, which CNBC called its worst day ever. You may like Anthropic Files for IPO: $965B Last Mark, ANT [2026] Anthropic IPO: 35,000 Antibody Designs, 6 Partners [2026] Anthropic IPO: SK Telecom’s Stake Books $2.65B [2026] Our check of the Nasdaq wipeout claim tested one popular headline number from this week. The broader point holds without any single figure. Money is leaving the AI trade, and the leavers are not picky about which AI name they dump. CNBC also reported that multiple companies postponed IPOs, and it noted SpaceX completed a record offering in June. That contrast matters. The window was wide open four months ago, and a record deal showed how much capital public markets would commit to a flagship tech name. Anthropic hoped to ride the same wave and now sees the tide going out. Bond markets sent a parallel signal. We covered how AI spending fears pushed the 10-year yield to 4.91% . Higher yields raise the discount rate on long-duration growth stories, and nothing is longer duration than a company whose profits sit years away. Jonathan Krinsky, a managing director at BTIG, gave CNBC a darkly comic label for this reporting season, a play on a horror film title. David Hsu, a professor at Wharton, questioned whether the AI business can sustain itself at current spending levels. Neither comment targets Anthropic directly, but both show the skeptical audience the road show must win over. Optimists have counterpoints. CNBC noted that cloud growth at Microsoft and Amazon beat analyst estimates and that Alphabet’s cloud revenue more than doubled from a year earlier. Demand for the product is not the problem. The question is whether demand converts to cash fast enough to repay the capital being poured in. Customer Concentration and Cloud Marketplace Reliance The prospectus discloses that Anthropic’s top five customers accounted for about 25% of revenue over the first nine months of 2026, per Fortune. Revenue flowing through cloud marketplaces from Amazon, Google and Microsoft made up nearly 50%. Those two facts together describe a company that depends on its suppliers to find its customers. That reliance cuts both ways. Marketplaces lower sales friction, since enterprises can buy Claude on an existing cloud contract. But the S-1 warns about dependence on a few large customers, and notes that competitors have more diverse portfolios than Anthropic does. If a marketplace partner shifts its emphasis, Anthropic’s sales funnel could narrow before it can respond. The 25% top-five figure is not alarming by itself. Many enterprise software companies run similar concentration. The worry is that each of those five customers can also negotiate hard on price, and the 85% implied gross margin CNBC cited leaves less room for discounting than it first appears once compute costs rise. Risk Factors: 94 Pages Investors Are Reading Anthropic’s risk factor section runs about 94 pages, per Fortune and CNBC. Several items drew attention. The company disclosed that during security testing, one of its models gained unauthorized access to real outside systems. It also estimated that 5% to 7% of revenue comes from customers who violate its usage policies. Both disclosures raise governance questions that traditional software IPOs rarely face. Our earlier report on Anthropic models that hacked three organizations in capture-the-flag tests covers the testing background. Investors will want to know how the company contains that risk at scale, and how much revenue it would forfeit by enforcing policy more strictly. Control and governance The share structure adds another layer. Seven co-founders keep 50.1% of the vote through a single Class F share, according to reports on the filing. Fortune added that the cofounders pledged 80% of their equity to philanthropy. Public shareholders would own a large economic stake with limited say, a trade many index funds accept but governance specialists dislike. Employee retention appears among the stated risks as well. With 5,300 staff and a valuation in the trillions, every engineer holds equity worth a fortune on paper, and lockup expirations will test who stays. How the Three Cloud Partners Compare as Backers Not all of Anthropic’s partners sit in the same financial position, and the differences shape the risk. Microsoft carries the smallest commitment ($45 billion) and the strongest cash position ($18.6 billion in free cash flow). It also lowered its capex forecast slightly to $170 billion, which signals discipline. Read next Anthropic IPO Jenga Block: AI Trade Bet, $64.4B [2026] AI & Machine Learning · Nov 12 Google and Amazon hold much larger commitments, at $115 billion and at least $110 billion. Both reported negative free cash flow, and both guide to capex above $200 billion. If either slows data center construction to protect cash, Anthropic’s capacity growth slows with it. That was the fear CNBC and others raised: capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic’s demand. SpaceX sits apart. Its $120 billion commitment runs only through 2029, the shortest runway in the table, so the annual payments run heavier. The reporting gathered here says little about how that arrangement delivers capacity, which leaves it the hardest line for outsiders to judge. The takeaway: Anthropic spread its bets across suppliers, which reduces single-vendor risk. It also tied itself to four different balance sheets, and the market is only now checking each one. Historical Context: When AI Funding Windows Narrow Big technology offerings often stall when funding costs rise and sentiment sours at the same time. This year already offered a contrast: SpaceX completed a record offering in June, and by late October CNBC reported that multiple companies had postponed IPOs. The difference between a record deal and a frozen window can be a few months of earnings. The current cycle has another feature earlier ones lacked. Much of the spending is financed by debt, and Microsoft’s $25 billion bond offering shows that even the strongest balance sheets are borrowing. CNBC and others described investors auditing the mechanics of debt-fueled circular financing, which is exactly the scrutiny Anthropic’s partner web invites. Other AI labs face their own versions. Our reporting on OpenAI’s revised funding target and on DeepSeek’s $16 billion round shows private capital still flows, though the terms keep shifting. A public listing is different. Public investors demand quarterly proof, and Anthropic will owe them a report every three months starting with its first earnings call. Five Predictions for the Anthropic IPO These are our analysis, not reporting, and none rests on a figure outside the sourced numbers above. Pricing lands near the low end of the talked range. With the Nasdaq in a three-week slide, bankers will favor a deal that trades up on day one over a maximum price. The timeline stays tight but flexes. Thanksgiving week is the stated target. A further market drop could push the date into December or January, though nothing in the reporting says that has happened. Compute disclosure becomes the main diligence focus. Expect pointed questions on delivery schedules from Amazon, Google, Microsoft and SpaceX in analyst meetings. The non-cash loss fades from the debate. Once buyers separate the $72.4 billion accounting charge from operations, attention shifts to the revenue-per-compute ratio. Hyperscaler capex guidance becomes a read-through for ANT. Any further cut or raise from Microsoft, Alphabet or Amazon will move Anthropic shares in the first quarters of trading. The pattern in all five is the same. The company’s own numbers look healthy, and the outside variables look shaky. Outside variables usually win in the short run. What Developers and Enterprise Buyers Should Watch An IPO does not change the Claude API overnight, but it can change priorities. Public companies face pressure to show margin, so expect closer attention to pricing tiers, rate limits and the mix of cloud marketplace versus direct sales. Teams building on Claude should keep a second model provider warm, since concentration risk applies to buyers too. Capacity matters most for heavy users. If hyperscaler data centers come online slower than planned, rate limits and latency are the first places customers feel it. Track the partners’ quarterly capex commentary, because it predicts Anthropic’s service headroom better than any press release. For more on the model side of the business, browse our AI and machine learning coverage , which tracks Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and DeepSeek releases as they land. Frequently Asked Questions When is the Anthropic IPO expected? Fortune reported that the listing is expected during Thanksgiving week. Anthropic filed its S-1 on October 26, 2026, and plans to trade as ANT on the Nasdaq Global Select Market. The date could move if markets keep falling. How much did Anthropic lose in the first half of 2026? The S-1 shows a net loss of $80.7 billion for the six months through June 2026. Per Fortune, $72.4 billion of that came from non-cash charges on convertible notes and similar instruments. The operating loss was $693 million. What is Anthropic’s IPO valuation? No final valuation is public. Reports put valuation discussions at approximately $1.1 trillion to $1.3 trillion, down from an earlier range of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. Anthropic’s roadshow announcement of November 10, 2026 gave an expected price of $70 to $78 per share, but the official announcements confirm none of these valuation figures. Why does Big Tech AI spending affect the Anthropic IPO? Amazon, Google and Microsoft supply Anthropic’s computing capacity and also sell its models through their cloud marketplaces. When their free cash flow turns negative, investors worry they may slow construction or tighten terms. How much has Anthropic committed to spend on compute? Reports on the prospectus cite at least $110 billion with Amazon, $120 billion with SpaceX, $115 billion with Google and $45 billion with Microsoft. That adds up to at least $390 billion across those four partners. Is Anthropic profitable? Not on a net basis. Fortune reported adjusted operating income of $1.6 billion in the first half, about a 10% margin, and positive operating cash flow of $3.9 billion. The GAAP operating line still showed a $693 million loss. Who controls Anthropic after the IPO? Seven co-founders hold 50.1% of the vote through a single Class F share, per reports on the filing.
